did_you_know.text: The Hebrew word malakh can mean either “messenger” or “angel,” so it may describe a human messenger or a divine one. Here, the context presents the angels as part of Jacob’s special encounter with God.
Mahanaim means “two camps,” a wordplay referring to Jacob’s camp and the angels’ camp. Later in the Bible, Mahanaim is also mentioned as a city in the Gilead region.
Seir, associated with the mountains of Edom, lies south and east of the Dead Sea. Jacob’s messengers therefore had to travel a considerable distance to reach Esau.
The verb garti is related to the Hebrew word ger, meaning a person living away from his homeland. Jacob emphasizes that he lived with Laban as an outsider, not as the master of the household.
Dividing the camp in two was an emergency strategy: if one camp were attacked, the other might survive. It shows both Jacob’s fear and his practical planning.
Jacob recalls that he once crossed the Jordan with only his staff, while now he has many people and possessions. The sentence expresses both gratitude and humility about the great change in his life.
The gift totaled 550 animals: goats, sheep, camels, cattle, and donkeys, including males and young animals. It was a very substantial gift, not merely a symbolic gesture.

Jacob told his servants to leave spaces between the herds, so the gift would arrive to Esau in several waves rather than all at once. This also created time and room for each meeting with the messengers.
The expression “I will appease him” describes an attempt at reconciliation, not only atonement in the modern sense. Jacob hopes the gift will soften Esau’s anger before they meet.

The Jabbok River is generally identified with the Zarqa River in Jordan, which flows into the Jordan from the east. It is one of the important geographical crossings in Jacob’s journey back to Canaan.

The verse calls Jacob’s opponent only “a man” and does not immediately explain who he is. This ambiguity has made the struggle open to many interpretations—as a physical or spiritual fight, or as a symbol of Jacob confronting his fears.
